Which ancient festival does she place be.The Panathenaia: The Panathenaia honoured the city goddess of Athens in high summer. Athena looks for a midwinter festival, when light is born out of the longest night.
Which ancient festival does she place be.The Thesmophoria: The Thesmophoria was the women's autumn festival of Demeter and Persephone, tied to sowing and the earth. It is not a midwinter birth of a sacred infant.
Which ancient festival does she place be.The Anthesteria: The Anthesteria was Dionysus' spring festival of flowers and new wine. The question asks for a winter festival set beside the Dionysia, a birth at the solstice.

Why does Christmas fall four days after.Four is the number of the elements of th: Athena works with Plato's three parts of the soul, not four elements. The four days are about what follows the solstice: the new light being made firm.
Why does Christmas fall four days after.Four marks the days of Persephone's desc: Persephone's descent lasts months, not four days, and Athena reads it through three names as three stages of the soul. Nothing there sets the date of Christmas.
Why does Christmas fall four days after.Four is the number of Plato's similes: Plato gives three similes in the Republic, the Sun, the Line and the Cave, so the count is wrong. They have nothing to do with the date of Christmas.

In her decoding of the Nativity, what do.The heart, seat of the logos: Athena links the heart with the spirited part and the emotions, not with logos. And a manger, a trough for beasts, points lower still, to where appetite lives.
In her decoding of the Nativity, what do.The head, seat of νοῦς: The head is the highest seat in the Timaeus, home of reason. A manger feeds animals, so it stands for a lower region, where the irrational powers are rooted.
In her decoding of the Nativity, what do.The throat, seat of speech: The throat is not where the Timaeus roots any power of the soul; it is the narrow neck between head and chest. A manger, where beasts feed, points lower.

What do the two animals at the manger co.The heart and the lungs: The heart and the lungs sit above the diaphragm, in the chest. The manger stands for the region below it, so its two animals are the organs that live there.
What do the two animals at the manger co.The two horses of the Phaedrus: The Phaedrus horses are another Platonic image of the soul's powers, but Athena does not use them here. The Nativity reading stays with the body, so the animals are organs.
What do the two animals at the manger co.Desire and anger: Close, since that region holds the irrational powers, but Athena names two organs, not two passions. The decoding is bodily: two animals, two organs below the solar plexus.

How does she read αἰών?.As 'a lifetime': That is the everyday dictionary sense, a span of life. Athena reads the word by its parts, and a span that ends is the opposite of what Athena finds there.
How does she read αἰών?.As 'the cycle of births': The cycle of births is the wheel of becoming that the soul longs to leave. Αἰών in Athena's reading points the other way, to what never enters that cycle.
How does she read αἰών?.As 'the age of iron': The age of iron is Hesiod's last and hardest age of humankind, a stretch of history. Athena's αἰών is not an age at all but what stays outside time.

Which mysteries had 'the Child' as the g.The Eleusinian Mysteries: The Eleusinian Mysteries centre on Demeter and Persephone's descent and return. Athena places their climax at the autumn equinox, not at a procession leading to a child.
Which mysteries had 'the Child' as the g.The Orphic rites of Thrace: The Orphic current is, for Athena, the heart-centred Dionysian way, and it encodes the second birth too. But it is not the rite Athena names for a procession to 'the Child'.
Which mysteries had 'the Child' as the g.The Delphic Pythia: The Pythia was Apollo's priestess at the Delphic oracle, not a mystery cult with a procession. Athena even says the seeker must become the oracle rather than visit one.

Which word does she link to ψεῦδος, fals.ψυχή, soul: Ψυχή shares the opening ψ, but Athena pairs it with ψύχω, to cool, not with falsehood. The link to ψεῦδος runs through the sound -ευδ-, not the first letter.
Which word does she link to ψεῦδος, fals.εὖ, well: Εὖ names the inner light of the Good in Athena's vocabulary, nearly the opposite of falsehood. The word hiding inside ψεῦδος carries its δ as well.
Which word does she link to ψεῦδος, fals.ψύχω, to cool: Ψύχω, to cool, is the word Athena joins to ψυχή: soul is nous that has cooled. It belongs to Athena's account of how soul forms, not to falsehood.

In Phaedo 64, what do philosophers pract.Only remembering and forgetting: Recollection is a real Platonic theme, and anamnesis matters to Athena, but it is not what Phaedo 64 names. That passage defines philosophy through the soul's release from the body.
In Phaedo 64, what do philosophers pract.Only questioning and answering: That describes Socratic dialogue, the method, not the practice Phaedo 64 names. Athena takes this passage as philosophy's first definition, and it is about letting go of the body.
In Phaedo 64, what do philosophers pract.Only measuring and counting: Measuring and counting belong to mathematics, which Plato values as a step upward. Phaedo 64 is not about number; it defines philosophy by its relation to death.

According to Proclus, how does the soul.By synthesis, adding virtues as garments: That reverses Proclus. Synthesis, putting on garments, is how the soul descends. Going up means taking off what was added, not dressing in more, even in virtues.
According to Proclus, how does the soul.By recollection of past lives: Recollection matters in Platonism, but Proclus' image here is about clothing, not memory. Remembering past lives would add more stories; the ascent Athena describes strips things away.
According to Proclus, how does the soul.By ecstatic dance: Nothing in Athena's reading of Proclus involves dance. The ascent is a stripping away, layer by layer, of what the soul put on as it came down.

In her Nativity reading, whom does Josep.The soul, which conceives: In Athena's decoding the soul is Mary, called Despoina, the one who conceives. Joseph is a different power, standing beside the soul and doubting its news.
In her Nativity reading, whom does Josep.The body, which protects: The body is not Joseph in Athena's reading. Joseph is the power that hears the soul's spiritual news and questions it, which points to thinking, not flesh.
In her Nativity reading, whom does Josep.The teacher, who guides: The teacher appears in Athena's birth story as the midwife who helps at the ripe hour. Joseph plays no such role; he is the doubter at the soul's side.

In the Theaetetus, with whom does Socrat.Only with those who have studied geometr: That recalls the legend over the Academy's door, 'let no one ignorant of geometry enter'. In the Theaetetus Socrates sets a different condition, about the soul's inner state.
In the Theaetetus, with whom does Socrat.Only with the young: Socrates does talk with the young Theaetetus here, but age is not his rule. A midwife can help only someone already carrying a child, whatever their age.
In the Theaetetus, with whom does Socrat.Only with those who pay: Taking fees was what the sophists did, and Socrates refused. His condition is not payment but a readiness already begun in the one he speaks with.

What is the Cave allegory Plato's answer.A question about the immortality of the: Immortality is argued in the Phaedo and in the myth of Er, not here. The Cave opens Book VII as an image of our nature with and without education.
What is the Cave allegory Plato's answer.A question about the best constitution: The Republic does discuss constitutions at length, but the Cave is not Plato's answer to that. It is offered for something more inward: what being educated really means.
What is the Cave allegory Plato's answer.A question about the origin of the cosmo: That is the subject of the Timaeus. The Cave is about the soul's journey from shadows to light, not about how the world came to be.

What does μύω mean?.To open the heart: Opening is the opposite of what μύω says. The word is about shutting, the gesture from which μύησις, initiation, takes its name.
What does μύω mean?.To kindle a flame: Kindling belongs to ἅπτω, which Athena links to touching truth and setting the inner fire alight. Μύω is a quieter verb, a shutting of the senses.
What does μύω mean?.To wander: Wandering is outward motion. Μύω points the other way, to stillness and to shutting the gates of the senses.

Whom does she read Artemis, Leto's first.The moon of emotion: Artemis is often joined to the moon, but in Athena's reading Leto's first child is a quality the soul must grow before Apollo's light appears, not an emotion.
Whom does she read Artemis, Leto's first.Wild nature: Wild nature is Artemis in popular myth, the huntress of the woods. Athena's reading is inward: Leto's first child is something the soul cultivates on its way out of Lethe.
Whom does she read Artemis, Leto's first.Justice: Justice is a key to the Good for Athena, but it is not the name given to Artemis. Athena reads Leto's first child through the sound of the name Artemis.

In the Odyssey, which books cover the sl.Books Α to Ν: Books Α to Ν carry Odysseus home: that is the return itself. The suitors wait in Ithaca, so their slaying fills the second half, after he lands.
In the Odyssey, which books cover the sl.Books Ι to Μ: Books Ι to Μ are the tales Odysseus tells at the Phaeacian court: the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens. That is still the journey, not the work done once home.
In the Odyssey, which books cover the sl.Books Α to Δ: Books Α to Δ are the Telemachy, with Telemachus seeking news of his father. Odysseus has not yet appeared, let alone reached Ithaca and faced the suitors.

What do the suitors stand for?.Rival philosophers: Athena reads the suitors inwardly, not as outside opponents. They occupy Odysseus' own house, as old tendencies still occupy the soul after the first awakening.
What do the suitors stand for?.The gods who oppose the soul: The suitors are mortals squatting in Odysseus' house, not gods. Athena reads them as what still occupies our own house after we come home.
What do the suitors stand for?.The senses: Athena does not treat the senses as enemies to slay; for Athena the philosopher purifies them and keeps them as allies.

What is her second definition of philoso.Measuring and dividing of truth: Measuring and dividing sound like method, the analytic mind at work. Athena's second definition is about contact and fire, not calculation.
What is her second definition of philoso.Recollection of the forms: Recollection is a real Platonic teaching, and Athena uses it, but it is not the second definition. That one pairs a verb of touch with a verb of fire.
What is her second definition of philoso.Dialectical refutation: Refutation, the elenchus, is Socrates' tool for clearing away false beliefs. Athena says the ancients' goal was to touch truth, not to win arguments.

Which two extremes come from misreading.Stoicism and Epicureanism: Those are two ancient schools, not misreadings. The misreadings Athena means are attitudes: if all is one, then nothing matters, or anything goes.
Which two extremes come from misreading.Dogmatism and scepticism: Those are positions about knowledge. The danger Athena names is ethical: taking 'all is one' as a licence for 'anything goes'.
Which two extremes come from misreading.Asceticism and ritualism: Those are ways of practising, not conclusions drawn from 'all is one'. The misreading Athena warns of drops the need for virtue altogether.

Persephone as 'bearer of light' correspo.Φερέπαφα: Φερέπαφα is bearer of touch, the third stage, when Persephone touches the immortal and returns to Demeter. Light comes before touch.
Persephone as 'bearer of light' correspo.Δέσποινα: Δέσποινα, 'Mistress', is a title, not one of the three names Athena reads as stages. In the Nativity reading Athena gives it to Mary, as the soul.
Persephone as 'bearer of light' correspo.Κόρη: Κόρη, 'the Maiden', is Persephone's common title, but it is not among the three names Athena reads as stages of the soul, and nothing in it speaks of light.

Whose Ascesis ends with the realisation.Plotinus: Athena does link that ending to Plotinus' highest vision, which is why the name tempts. But the book is a modern Greek one; Plotinus wrote the Enneads.
Whose Ascesis ends with the realisation.Dionysios Solomos: Solomos is Greece's national poet, author of the Hymn to Liberty, and wrote no Ascesis. The book belongs to the writer Athena calls the Heraclitus of the modern era.
Whose Ascesis ends with the realisation.Proclus: Proclus is a Neoplatonist Athena often quotes, but he wrote commentaries and hymns, not the Ascesis. That book, subtitled Salvatores Dei, is twentieth-century.

Alexander said he owed εὖ ζῆν to whom?.His father Philip: Philip was Alexander's father, so in Athena's telling he gave Alexander life itself, ζῆν. Living well came from someone else.
Alexander said he owed εὖ ζῆν to whom?.Diogenes: Diogenes appears in the same story as the man Alexander envied, not the one he thanked. The debt for εὖ ζῆν was to a teacher.
Alexander said he owed εὖ ζῆν to whom?.Plato: Plato died when Alexander was a boy of about eight and never taught him. Alexander's teacher was Plato's own pupil.

Whom does she say Alexander would rather.Achilles: Alexander revered Achilles as his heroic model, so the guess is natural. But Athena's point in this story is the reverse: the conqueror envied someone who owned nothing.
Whom does she say Alexander would rather.Socrates: Socrates is the philosopher Athena returns to most, but he is not in this anecdote. Alexander's remark was about a man he met in Corinth, living in a jar.
Whom does she say Alexander would rather.Heracles: Alexander claimed descent from Heracles, but this story is not about heroic labours. It is about a ruler who saw a freedom no conquest could give.

What does she define εὖ ζῆν as?.Success in the polis: Success is exactly what Athena says εὖ ζῆν is not. Care for the common good belongs to it, but as a fruit of inner freedom, not of public standing.
What does she define εὖ ζῆν as?.Health and wealth together: Those are conditions that help, and they can be lost. Athena separates living well from anything that depends on circumstances.
What does she define εὖ ζῆν as?.Fame that outlives death: Fame lives in other people's mouths, outside you. Athena names fame among the things εὖ ζῆν is not.

Which word does she link to βίος?.βαίνω, to walk: Βαίνω, to walk, shares only the opening β with βίος. The word Athena pairs with life speaks of force and strain, not of moving from place to place.
Which word does she link to βίος?.βλέπω, to see: Βλέπω, to see, would make life a kind of vision, but that is not Athena's link. Athena hears βίος as close to strain and compulsion.
Which word does she link to βίος?.βουλή, will: Will matters elsewhere in Athena's teaching, but not here. For βίος Athena points to a word of force: life lived under pressure.

Which god does she link to ζῆν?.Hermes, symbol of speech: Hermes is the god of speech and messages, and Athena gives him the role of guide of souls. His name has no echo of ζῆν.
Which god does she link to ζῆν?.Apollo, symbol of light: Apollo is Athena's god of awakening and light, but his name holds no ζ. The link to ζῆν runs through sound, and only one god's name sounds like it.
Which god does she link to ζῆν?.Dionysus, symbol of the vine: Dionysus belongs to the vine and to ecstasy, but his name does not sound like ζῆν. Athena's link runs through an old name of the king of the gods.

What Stoic term does she give for the in.ἐκπύρωσις: Ἐκπύρωσις is Stoic too, but it names the periodic burning of the whole universe, a cosmic event. Inner peace is a state of the soul.
What Stoic term does she give for the in.κάθαρσις: Κάθαρσις is purification, central to Athena's teaching but not a Stoic name for calm. It is a process that clears the way, not the peace itself.
What Stoic term does she give for the in.ἐποχή: Ἐποχή is suspension of judgment, above all a Sceptic term. It is a mental practice, not the settled calm Athena places at the heart of εὖ ζῆν.

In her reading of the Cave, what do the.The capacity for work: Hands do suggest work, and Athena does say awakening must become work. But in the Cave the free hands point to something deeper: what no chain can bind.
In her reading of the Cave, what do the.The senses: The senses are bound up with what the prisoners see and hear on the wall, which is the trouble. The free hands stand for what remains unbound.
In her reading of the Cave, what do the.Charity toward others: Charity is a fruit of awakening, but it is not what Athena reads in the hands. The point is that the prisoner can still choose, even in chains.

Whose reframing 'depressed means deep re.Marcus Aurelius: Marcus Aurelius is Athena's Stoic for ἀπάθεια and for freedom even in prison. This wordplay on 'depressed' is modern and English, not his.
Whose reframing 'depressed means deep re.Carl Jung: Jung appears in Athena's teaching for archetypes and shadow work. The pun on 'deep rest' comes from an actor, not a psychologist.
Whose reframing 'depressed means deep re.Kazantzakis: Kazantzakis wrote in Greek, and this is an English pun, turning 'depressed' into 'deep rest'. Athena cites a modern actor for it.

How does she explain the word 'paradox'?.πάρα δόξα, much glory: Δόξα can mean glory, but here it means opinion, and παρά means beside or against, not 'much'. A paradox is something that runs past common belief.
How does she explain the word 'paradox'?.παρὰ τὸν δόκον, beside the beam: Δόκος, a beam, only looks like δόξα. The word is built on δόξα, opinion, which Athena places inside the cave.
How does she explain the word 'paradox'?.πᾶς ἀδοξία, total obscurity: That splits the word in the wrong place. Παρα- is a preposition, not πᾶς, and the second half is δόξα, opinion, not ἀδοξία.

What does she find inside γνῶσις?.γῆ, earth, plus νόμος: Earth and law match a few letters, but they miss Athena's point, which ties γνῶσις to the gestation theme running through the whole talk.
What does she find inside γνῶσις?.γάμος, marriage, plus νόστος: Marriage and homecoming are rich words in Athena's teaching, but νόστος does not sit inside γνῶσις. The ν there is read as mind, not as return.
What does she find inside γνῶσις?.γένος, kind, plus νόσος: Γένος starts close, but νόσος, illness, would make knowledge a disease. Athena reads the ν-sound as mind, the faculty that knows.

Where was Diotima, Socrates' teacher, fr.Miletus in Ionia: Miletus is the Ionian city of Thales and the first natural philosophers. Plato gives Diotima a different home, inland in the Peloponnese.
Where was Diotima, Socrates' teacher, fr.Elea in Italy: Elea is Parmenides' city in southern Italy. Diotima, as Plato presents her in the Symposium, comes from the Peloponnese.
Where was Diotima, Socrates' teacher, fr.Delphi in Phocis: Diotima was a priestess, which makes Delphi tempting, but Plato does not tie her to Apollo's oracle. Her city lies in the Peloponnese.

What does the epithet λυσιμελής mean?.Honey-sweet: The μελ- here is μέλος, limb, not μέλι, honey. Λυσι- comes from λύω, to loosen: eros undoes the body's strength.
What does the epithet λυσιμελής mean?.Bitter-sweet: Bitter-sweet is γλυκύπικρος, the word Sappho sets right beside λυσιμελής in the same line about Eros. They are two different epithets.
What does the epithet λυσιμελής mean?.Gold-crowned: Gold-crowned would be χρυσοστέφανος. Nothing in λυσιμελής speaks of gold; it joins 'loosen' and 'limb'.

Which word does she say 'has ἔρως inside.ἀρετή, virtue: Ἀρετή begins with ἀρ-, not ἐρ-, and Athena reads it as 'ever-flowing', ἀεὶ ῥεῖν. Its link is with flow, not with eros.
Which word does she say 'has ἔρως inside.ἐρημία, solitude: Ἐρημία does start with ἐρ-, which makes it tempting. But the word Athena opens up names a state the heart wants for everyone, not being alone.
Which word does she say 'has ἔρως inside.ἑορτή, feast: Ἑορτή sounds close, and Athena does call εὖ ζῆν a feast. But eros, for Athena, lives inside the word for being unbound.

What does νόησις mean in the Cratylus re.νοῦ θέσις, the setting of the mind: That would make thought something set down and fixed. The Cratylus reading has no θέσις in it; it is about movement, not placement.
What does νόησις mean in the Cratylus re.νόμου ἴσις, equality of law: Law and equality belong to politics, not to this etymology. The Cratylus reading is about the mind's appetite, not civic order.
What does νόησις mean in the Cratylus re.νόστου ἔσις, the longing for home: Longing for home suits Athena's love of νόστος, but this Cratylus reading looks forward, not back to where we came from.

Which virtue does she say Aristotle call.σωφροσύνη, moderation: Moderation is a classic virtue, but it restrains. The virtue Athena puts first, in Aristotle's name, is a brave and noble readiness to act.
Which virtue does she say Aristotle call.φρόνησις, prudence: Φρόνησις is practical wisdom, which Aristotle counts as an intellectual virtue, not a moral one. The question asks which moral virtue comes first.
Which virtue does she say Aristotle call.δικαιοσύνη, justice: Justice is central to Athena's teaching and to the Republic, but here Athena names a different virtue for Aristotle, one of brave and noble spirit.

What does the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβ.Flee shame: That reverses the maxim. Σέβου means respect or revere; fleeing shame is what the ego does when it hides from its own conscience.
What does the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβ.Nothing in excess: That is μηδὲν ἄγαν, a different Delphic maxim. Here the word is αἰσχύνη, shame, and the verb asks you to honour it.
What does the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβ.Know the right moment: That is καιρὸν γνῶθι, another maxim of the Seven Sages. This one names shame, αἰσχύνη, and tells you how to treat it.

What one sentence would she put on a bil.μηδὲν ἄγαν, nothing in excess: Μηδὲν ἄγαν was carved at Delphi too, but it is not Athena's choice. Athena would put up the precept that turns the soul's eye inward.
What one sentence would she put on a bil.πάντα ῥεῖ, all flows: Πάντα ῥεῖ is the saying tied to Heraclitus, whom Athena loves. But for a billboard Athena picks a Delphic command, not a description of flux.
What one sentence would she put on a bil.καιρὸν γνῶθι, know the moment: Καιρὸν γνῶθι shares the γνῶθι, which makes it close. But Athena's motto asks you to know yourself, not the moment.

Whom does she follow in deriving the Tit.Plotinus: Plotinus is Athena's source for the seer being one with the seen. This etymology comes from a later Neoplatonist whom Athena calls 'fully awakened'.
Whom does she follow in deriving the Tit.Hesiod: Hesiod does tie the name to straining, as a reproach from Ouranos. But Athena reads the Titans as inner tendencies, and for that follows a later Neoplatonist.
Whom does she follow in deriving the Tit.Porphyry: Porphyry was Plotinus' pupil and editor, a Neoplatonist too, but Athena credits this reading of the Titans to a later head of the Athenian school.

What subtitle of the Republic does she s.On the Soul: Περὶ ψυχῆς is the title of Aristotle's work on the soul. The Republic covers the soul, but its subtitle names the question it opens with in Piraeus.
What subtitle of the Republic does she s.On the Good: The Good is the Republic's summit, not its subtitle. The dialogue opens in Piraeus with a different question, and the subtitle names that one.
What subtitle of the Republic does she s.On Nature: Περὶ φύσεως is the title given to many Presocratic works. The Republic's subtitle names the question Socrates pursues from the first book on.

In what order do Plato's three similes a.Cave, Line, Sun: That reverses the order. The Cave comes last, opening Book VII, after the Sun and the Line at the end of Book VI.
In what order do Plato's three similes a.Line, Sun, Cave: The Line comes after the Sun, because it orders what the Sun simile taught. Only the Cave is in its right place here.
In what order do Plato's three similes a.Sun, Cave, Line: The Cave is the third simile, not the second. The Line follows the Sun directly, still in Book VI, and the Cave opens Book VII.

What does she call the Sun simile?.Platonic geometry of the soul: Close in spirit, since the name is mathematical, but it is not Athena's phrase. Athena's word points to measured relations between terms, as in a triangle, not to the soul's geometry.
What does she call the Sun simile?.The solar hymn: A hymn praises; a simile compares. Athena names it with a mathematical word because the Sun simile works by proportion, setting one set of terms against another.
What does she call the Sun simile?.The ladder of light: A ladder suggests climbing step by step, which fits the Line or Diotima's ascent better. Athena's name for the Sun simile is mathematical, about how its terms relate.

In the Sun simile, what is the fourth te.The Idea of the Good: The Good is the source in the simile, paired with the sun itself, so it is one of the main terms. The 'third kind' is what joins seeing and seen.
In the Sun simile, what is the fourth te.Heat: Heat belongs to the sun too, and Athena reads it as eros, but Plato's 'third kind' is what lets the eye see its objects. Heat does not do that.
In the Sun simile, what is the fourth te.The soul: The soul corresponds to the eye in the simile, the one who sees. The 'third kind' sits between eye and object and makes seeing possible.

What is the soul called as the counterpa.ἡλιοειδής, sun-like: Ἡλιοειδής is Plato's word for the eye, the sense organ most like the sun. The soul's counterpart takes its name from what the sun stands for, one level up.
What is the soul called as the counterpa.θεοειδής, god-like: Θεοειδής, god-like, is a fine word but not the one in the simile. Plato's parallel runs from the sun to the Good, so the soul is named after the Good.
What is the soul called as the counterpa.πυροειδής, fire-like: Fire-like suits Athena's image of a little fiery sun within, which is why it tempts. But the word follows the simile's logic: sun for the eye, the Good for the soul.

In the Sun simile, what is the heat of t.Justice: Justice is the other key to the Good for Athena, but in the Sun simile it is not given as the heat. Heat is the warming, drawing force.
In the Sun simile, what is the heat of t.Courage: Courage belongs to the spirited part of the soul, a virtue of warrior and philosopher. It is not what Athena reads as the warmth pouring from the Good.
In the Sun simile, what is the heat of t.Memory: Memory, as recollection, sits nearer to knowing, the light side of the simile. Heat is what warms and draws us, not what we recall.

What is the first trait of the ideal phi.Being strong in body: Plato does want guardians trained in gymnastics, but bodily strength is not the first trait Athena stresses. The leader must first be in love with the Good.
What is the first trait of the ideal phi.Being of noble birth: Noble birth is not what Plato asks of a philosopher-leader, and Athena puts love of the Good first. A ruler is chosen for nature and formation, not family.
What is the first trait of the ideal phi.Being skilled in rhetoric: Rhetoric is the art of sophists and politicians, which Plato distrusted. Athena's first trait is about what the leader loves, not how well they speak.

What does Plato call release from the ca.κάθαρσις καὶ μάθησις: Purification and learning are real themes, but they are not Plato's words at 515c. He pairs a word for loosening chains with a word from medicine.
What does Plato call release from the ca.ἀνάμνησις καὶ λήθη: That pairs recollection with its opposite, forgetting, so it could not name a release. Plato's phrase joins two words for setting free and making well.
What does Plato call release from the ca.μέθεξις καὶ μίμησις: Participation and imitation describe how things relate to the forms. Plato's phrase for leaving the chains is about freeing and curing, not metaphysics.

What are the two keys she names for cont.Reason and faith: Reason and faith are a medieval pairing. Athena's two keys are not faculties of knowing; they are a love and a virtue.
What are the two keys she names for cont.Prayer and fasting: Prayer and fasting are religious practices. Athena's keys come from the Republic itself: a force of love and a virtue of right order.
What are the two keys she names for cont.Memory and imagination: Memory and imagination are powers of the mind. Athena's two keys are what moves the heart and what sets the soul in order.

What is the inner, 'fiery key' definitio.Giving each what is owed: That is Simonides' definition, which Polemarchus defends in Book I. Athena places it in the middle cave, as give-and-take, not as the inner key.
What is the inner, 'fiery key' definitio.The advantage of the stronger: That is Thrasymachus' claim in Book I, which Socrates refutes. It is a cynical view of power, not an inner state of the soul.
What is the inner, 'fiery key' definitio.Obeying the laws of the city: Law-abiding justice belongs to the outer level, the court system of the deep cave in Athena's map. The inner key concerns the soul's own order.

Which definition of justice does she giv.Justice is the advantage of the stronger: That is Thrasymachus, who bursts in after Polemarchus in Book I. Polemarchus defends an older idea, about paying back what is owed.
Which definition of justice does she giv.Justice is doing one's own: Doing one's own is the inner key, the definition Socrates reaches in Book IV. Polemarchus never gets that far; his view stays at the middle level.
Which definition of justice does she giv.Justice is a convention: Justice as convention is the social-contract account Glaucon lays out in Book II. Polemarchus speaks earlier, in Book I, and his view is about debts.

In the Cratylus, what is δίκαιον?.What is agreed by the people: That would make justice a human convention. The Cratylus finds a cosmic motion in the word, not a vote.
In the Cratylus, what is δίκαιον?.What the gods decree: Divine decree is a picture of command from above. The Cratylus reading has no decree in it; it hears motion in the word.
In the Cratylus, what is δίκαιον?.What is equal in measure: Equality is a common modern picture of justice, and Athena does speak of balance. But the Cratylus etymology is about movement through all things, not equal shares.

What does she link πρόνοια to?.πρὸ τοῦ χρόνου, before time, and Kronos: Πρόνοια holds νοῦς, not χρόνος, as its second part. The goddess in the word is the goddess of wisdom, honoured at Delphi as Pronaia.
What does she link πρόνοια to?.πρὸς νόμον, toward law, and Themis: Themis suits justice, the topic of the talk, but πρόνοια is πρό plus νοῦς, not πρός plus νόμος. Its goddess is the one of wisdom.
What does she link πρόνοια to?.πρὸ νόστου, before the return, and Herme: Νόστος is a word Athena loves, but it is not inside πρόνοια. The word is built on νοῦς, mind, and its goddess is the one born from Zeus's head.

Where does she say there were theatres,.In all the gymnasia: Gymnasia trained the body and hosted teaching, but Athena's point is about healing. The theatres stood where people went to be cured.
Where does she say there were theatres,.In every agora: The agora was the place of speech and trade. Athena's point is that theatre was a cure, so it stood where the sick came for healing.
Where does she say there were theatres,.At every oracle: Delphi did have a theatre, but Athena's point is medical: theatre heals, so it stood at the sanctuaries of the healing god.

What did Diogenes ask for at his burial?.To be cremated with his lamp: The lamp belongs to another Diogenes story, his search for an honest man. His burial wish was a joke about the world turning upside down.
What did Diogenes ask for at his burial?.To be thrown to the dogs: Close: some ancient accounts do say Diogenes asked to be left unburied for the animals. But the version Athena tells is about how he should lie in the grave.
What did Diogenes ask for at his burial?.To be buried at the crossroads: Nothing in the story Athena tells involves a crossroads. His request was about which way his body should face.

Which Heraclitus fragment is the core te.B52, Aion as a child: Athena does build on B52, Aion as a child at play, but it is not the core text of this lesson. Part A is anchored in the fragment on the cosmos as fire.
Which Heraclitus fragment is the core te.B118, the dry soul: B118 on the dry soul comes near the end of Part A, as a consequence. The core text, written on the board, is about the cosmos itself.
Which Heraclitus fragment is the core te.B91, the river: B91 is the river fragment: you cannot step twice into the same river. It is about flux, while this lesson's core text is about what the cosmos is.

What does she call Heraclitus, instead o.The weeping: 'The weeping philosopher' is a later nickname, set against laughing Democritus. Athena's word is the opposite of 'dark', not a mood.
What does she call Heraclitus, instead o.The obscure: The obscure is just 'the dark' in other words, ὁ σκοτεινός. Athena turns the nickname around rather than repeating it.
What does she call Heraclitus, instead o.The proud: Heraclitus was famous for his haughtiness, but Athena's renaming answers 'the dark'. It names what Athena finds in him, not his temper.

What kind of reader did Socrates say Her.A Delphic priest: Delphi belongs to Apollo too, which makes it close, but Socrates' joke is about depth: the book needs someone who can dive and come back up.
What kind of reader did Socrates say Her.An Eleusinian initiate: Initiation fits the mystery in Heraclitus, but Socrates' image is of a swimmer, someone who can go deep and not drown.
What kind of reader did Socrates say Her.A Spartan general: A Spartan general suggests endurance, but Socrates' quip is about depth. The reader of Heraclitus must dive, like the famous divers of Delos.

How does she read ἀΐδιος?.As ἀ-ἰδεῖν, unseen: Unseen is the old etymology of Hades' name. Athena reads ἀΐδιος, eternal, through a word for 'always', not through sight.
How does she read ἀΐδιος?.As Ἅιδου, of Hades: The sounds are close, and Heraclitus does say Hades and Dionysus are one. But ἀΐδιος means everlasting, and Athena reads it as permanence, not the underworld.
How does she read ἀΐδιος?.As ἀεὶ ἰδεῖν, always seeing: Very close: the ἀεί is right. But the second part is ἴδιον, one's own or the same, not ἰδεῖν, to see. The point is sameness, not vision.

To which word does she link Ἑστία?.ἵστημι, to stand: Standing suits a fixed hearth, so it tempts. But Athena links Hestia to the being of things: in the Orphic sequence Hestia is the essence that dreams the many.
To which word does she link Ἑστία?.ἐσθής, garment: A garment is something put on, while Hestia is what remains under every garment. Athena reads Hestia as the soul's core, not its clothing.
To which word does she link Ἑστία?.ἑστίασις, feast: Ἑστίασις, a feast, actually comes from ἑστία, the hearth where meals were shared. It descends from the word; it is not the deeper link Athena draws.

Which verb means both 'to touch' and 'to.καίω: Καίω means to burn or set alight, but it carries no sense of touch. Only one verb holds both meanings, which lets Athena join touch and fire.
Which verb means both 'to touch' and 'to.λάμπω: Λάμπω means to shine, giving off light rather than catching fire, and it never means to touch.
Which verb means both 'to touch' and 'to.φλέγω: Φλέγω means to burn or blaze, but not to touch. Athena needs a verb that does both at once.

Whom does she credit with the 'sea of tr.Thales: Thales made water the first principle, which is why a sea suggests him. But this image comes from the Symposium, from a speech about the summit of love.
Whom does she credit with the 'sea of tr.Anaximander: Anaximander's principle was the boundless, ἄπειρον, not a sea. The image Athena uses comes from the Symposium.
Whom does she credit with the 'sea of tr.Parmenides: Parmenides gave a goddess's way of truth, but no sea. Athena takes this image from Socrates' teacher in the Symposium.

Which Greek physicist does she cite on t.Dimitris Nanopoulos: Nanopoulos is a well-known Greek physicist, but he is not the one Athena cites on the brain's 'ontological algorithm'.
Which Greek physicist does she cite on t.Kostas Krimizis: That is not the scientist Athena cites. Athena takes the brain's 'ontological algorithm' from a Greek astrophysicist who writes on cosmology for a wide public.
Which Greek physicist does she cite on t.Georgios Papadopoulos: That name belongs to no physicist Athena cites. The source for the brain's 'ontological algorithm' is a Greek astrophysicist, Manolis Danezis.

How does Heraclitus describe the Logos,.Private to each soul: Heraclitus names this as the error of the many, not the truth. Athena even insists on the spelling ξυνός, shared, not ξινός, sour.
How does Heraclitus describe the Logos,.Hidden in the gods alone: Heraclitus' Logos is not kept by the gods alone; it runs through the whole cosmos and through each of us, even when we fail to notice it.
How does Heraclitus describe the Logos,.Born anew in each age: The Logos does not come and go with the ages. Heraclitus calls it everlasting, ἐόντος ἀεί, and the same for all.

Where does she say the word 'metaphysics.Plato's lectures on the Ideas: Plato never used the word. It is a library label that came long after both Plato and Aristotle.
Where does she say the word 'metaphysics.Pythagorean number lore: The Pythagoreans had no such category. The word began as an editor's label for where certain books were placed.
Where does she say the word 'metaphysics.Plotinus' Enneads: Porphyry did arrange the Enneads, but 'metaphysics' did not come from them. It names a group of Aristotle's writings and where they were shelved.

From which verb does she derive μονάς?.μόνος, alone: Μόνος, alone, is the usual derivation and a natural guess. Athena prefers a verb, so the Monad becomes an act of abiding, not just being single.
From which verb does she derive μονάς?.μανθάνω, to learn: Μανθάνω shares the μ and ν sounds but means to learn, which belongs to the knower, not the source. Athena's verb describes what the Monad does.
From which verb does she derive μονάς?.μοῖρα, fate: Μοῖρα, fate, is a share given out, and Athena does use it for the local point of view. But the Monad is named for abiding, not for being allotted.

Which line of Parmenides does she quote?.All things flow: All things flow is the saying tied to Heraclitus. Parmenides denies change, so it could hardly be his.
Which line of Parmenides does she quote?.Man is the measure of all things: That is Protagoras the sophist, whose relativism Plato attacks. Parmenides speaks of being, not of human measure.
Which line of Parmenides does she quote?.Nothing comes from nothing: That idea follows from Parmenides' argument and later became a maxim, but it is not the line Athena quotes. Athena's line is about thinking.

In her chain of vehicles, what is the ve.The body: The body is one step lower: it carries the soul. Nous needs a finer vehicle than flesh.
In her chain of vehicles, what is the ve.The aura: Athena does speak of the aura, the part of the soul that lies outside the body, but it is not a separate rung in the chain of vehicles.
In her chain of vehicles, what is the ve.The breath: Breath is not part of Athena's chain of vehicles, which runs through three levels, each one carrying the level above.

Which Heraclitus fragment says the dry s.B30: B30 is the ever-living fire, the core text of Part A. The dry soul comes in a later fragment.
Which Heraclitus fragment says the dry s.B52: B52 is Aion as a child playing draughts. The dry soul is a different fragment.
Which Heraclitus fragment says the dry s.B62: B62 is the riddle of immortals and mortals living each other's death. It is not about the dry soul.

How does she explain αὔη, dry?.αὐγή, the dawn light: Αὐγή, dawn light, is close in sound, and light matters to Athena. But Athena reads αὔη by its sense, dry, as what the rain has not touched.
How does she explain αὔη, dry?.αὔω, to shout: Αὔω, to shout, shares the letters but not the sense. Dryness has to do with water, and Athena's reading turns on rain.
How does she explain αὔη, dry?.αὐτός, oneself: Αὐτός sounds close, but dryness has nothing to do with self in Athena's reading. The etymology is about a soul not soaked by the passions.

What did Pythagoras answer to 'what is b.ἁρμονία: Harmony is a great Pythagorean word, so the guess is natural. But in the Pythagorean sayings harmony answers a different question: 'what is most beautiful?'
What did Pythagoras answer to 'what is b.ἀριθμός: In the Pythagorean sayings number answers 'what is wisest?', not 'what is best?'.
What did Pythagoras answer to 'what is b.σιωπή: Silence was a famous Pythagorean discipline for new pupils, but it is a practice, not the answer to 'what is best?'.

What best modern Greek word for νοῦς doe.μυαλό, brain: Μυαλό is the everyday word for brain or mind, the organ. Athena's νοῦς is far more than an organ in the head.
What best modern Greek word for νοῦς doe.λογική, logic: Λογική is reasoning, one function of the mind. Νοῦς for Athena is wider than logic; reasoning works within it.
What best modern Greek word for νοῦς doe.ψυχισμός, psyche: Ψυχισμός names the psyche, the soul's inner life. In Athena's chain the soul is the vehicle of νοῦς, not νοῦς itself.

What does 'I'm not political' amount to,.A neutral private choice: There is no neutral ground here, because for the Greeks politics is human nature. Opting out is still a way of taking part, by leaving the field to others.
What does 'I'm not political' amount to,.A sign of wisdom: Athena sees it the other way: withdrawing makes one an ἰδιώτης, cut off from the whole, which Athena calls a disease, not wisdom.
What does 'I'm not political' amount to,.A Stoic withdrawal: The Stoics taught inner freedom, yet Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire. For Athena no one steps outside the political, since it is our nature.

What does she call today's depoliticisat.Secularisation: Secularisation is about religion's place in society. Athena's pairing is about nature: losing the sense that we belong to a rational cosmos.
What does she call today's depoliticisat.Globalisation: Globalisation is economic and cultural spread. Athena's twin is about our relationship to nature, not markets.
What does she call today's depoliticisat.Urbanisation: Cities may cut us off from fields, but Athena's point is deeper than geography. The twin of depoliticisation is a change in how we see nature itself.

To whom does she attribute the term biop.Hannah Arendt: Arendt wrote on the human condition and totalitarianism, but Athena credits biopolitics to a French thinker who studied how modern power manages bodies.
To whom does she attribute the term biop.Jean-Jacques Rousseau: Rousseau is the social-contract thinker of the eighteenth century. Biopolitics is a twentieth-century name for that era's shift to governing bodies.
To whom does she attribute the term biop.Max Weber: Weber analysed bureaucracy and the 'disenchantment of the world'. Biopolitics, the management of life and bodies, is credited to someone else.

Which three institutions does she say we.The parliament, the court and the school: Courts and schools are far older than the eighteenth century. Athena's three are institutions that confine and manage bodies, the ones Foucault studied.
Which three institutions does she say we.The bank, the factory and the stock mark: Those are economic institutions. Athena's three belong to biopolitics: places that confine, treat and discipline the body.
Which three institutions does she say we.The museum, the library and the universi: Libraries and universities long predate that era. Athena names institutions of confinement and care for bodies, not of learning.

What does she call the lawgiver?.νομοφύλαξ, a guardian of law: Νομοφύλαξ, guardian of the laws, is a real office in Plato's Laws, but it guards what already exists. Athena's word says the lawgiver forms character.
What does she call the lawgiver?.δημαγωγός, a leader of the people: A demagogue leads the crowd, and the word soon turned negative. Athena's term is about shaping the soul through law, not swaying people.
What does she call the lawgiver?.ἐπίτροπος, a steward: A steward manages on someone else's behalf. Athena's term names a deeper task: law as something that moulds ἦθος.

Aristotle's citizen partakes in which tw.Paying taxes and voting: That is the thin modern picture of citizenship. Aristotle's citizen takes part in the city's courts and offices, not just its ballots.
Aristotle's citizen partakes in which tw.Fighting and farming: Those are tasks many people did, including those who were not citizens. Aristotle defines the citizen by a share in courts and office.
Aristotle's citizen partakes in which tw.Worship and festivals: Festivals were part of city life, but Aristotle does not define the citizen by them. His definition is about sharing power: deciding cases and holding office.

How does she derive ἀγορά?.ἀγρός plus ὁράω: Field and seeing match a few letters, but Athena hears in ἀγορά a verb of speaking, which fits a place of argument.
How does she derive ἀγορά?.ἀγών plus ῥέω: Contest and flowing are tempting, since debate can be a contest. But Athena's second element is a verb of speech, not of flow.
How does she derive ἀγορά?.ἀγαθόν plus ὥρα: Good and hour are lovely words, but the split does not work. Athena reads the second part as speaking, εἴρω.

What does she call the four-yearly elect.A sacred feast: A feast is joyful and shared, which elections rarely are. Athena's word is critical: the vote has become a performance standing in for real participation.
What does she call the four-yearly elect.A civic oath: An oath binds you to act. Athena's point is that the vote has become a ceremony, a gesture every four years in place of ongoing participation.
What does she call the four-yearly elect.A people's tribunal: A tribunal judges, which is close to Aristotle's citizen, but judging together is exactly what Athena says modern elections lack.

How does she break down the word ἐμπειρί.ἐν + πῦρ: 'within the fire': Fire is everywhere in Athena's teaching, so the guess makes sense, but the root here is πεῖρα, read through πέρας, limit. Experience has edges.
How does she break down the word ἐμπειρί.ἐμ + πείθω: 'persuaded within': Πείθω, to persuade, is not in the word. Athena's point needs a root of boundary, because the infinite cannot be held inside one.
How does she break down the word ἐμπειρί.ἐν + πόρος: 'within the passage': Πόρος, passage, belongs to ἀπορία, not here. Athena reads ἐμπειρία through limit: anything experienced has a border.

What does she say the Greek tradition ca.ἔκστασις, standing outside oneself: Ἔκστασις, standing outside oneself, implies going somewhere else. Athena's word is quieter: often nothing happens, and you see what was always there.
What does she say the Greek tradition ca.ἐνθουσιασμός, being filled with a god: Being filled with a god is a real Greek state, prophetic or poetic. But it suggests something entering you, while for Athena nothing new has to come in.
What does she say the Greek tradition ca.κάθαρσις, purification: Κάθαρσις is purification, a preparation on the path. The name for awakening itself is a word of seeing, with the same root as θέατρον.

Which four attributes does she give the.ἄπειρον, ἀγέννητον, ἄφθαρτον, ἀκίνητον: These are classic negations, close to Parmenides' account of being. But Athena's four deny something else: that the One can be reached by our words or our minds.
Which four attributes does she give the.ἀγαθόν, καλόν, ἀληθές, δίκαιον: Good, beautiful, true and just are positive names. Athena's attributes work the apophatic way, saying only what the One is not.
Which four attributes does she give the.νοῦς, ψυχή, φύσις, ὕλη: Those are the levels that flow out of the One: mind, soul, nature, matter. They are its emanations, not its attributes.

How does she explain ἀμέθεκτον?.The One cannot be measured: Being beyond measure fits the One, but that is not this word. Ἀμέθεκτον comes from μέθεξις, participation: nothing takes the One in as an ingredient.
How does she explain ἀμέθεκτον?.The One has no beginning: That would be ἀγέννητον or ἄναρχον. Ἀμέθεκτον is built on μετέχω, to share in, so it is about mixing, not origins.
How does she explain ἀμέθεκτον?.The One cannot be named: That is ἄρρητον, the first of the four attributes. Ἀμέθεκτον is the last, and it is about mixing, not naming.

What name did the Pythagoreans use for t.Zeus: Zeus is, for Athena, mind in its creative work, dividing and returning. The Pythagorean code name belongs to the god of light, Delphi and awakening.
What name did the Pythagoreans use for t.Hestia: Hestia is the hearth at the centre, Athena's image of essence and of the Circle of the Same. But the Pythagoreans' name for the One was another god's.
What name did the Pythagoreans use for t.Phanes: Phanes is the Orphic first-born god of light, a fine guess. But Plutarch and Plotinus report a different name, one Athena reads letter by letter.

What is her favourite word for the One's.ἀκτινοβολία: Ἀκτινοβολία is radiation, rays thrown outward, with a modern scientific ring. Athena prefers a word built on φῶς and αὐγή, without beams flying off.
What is her favourite word for the One's.λαμπηδών: Λαμπηδών is brilliance or flash, from λάμπω, like a gleam on a surface. Athena's favourite word is built on φῶς and the glow of dawn.
What is her favourite word for the One's.φωσφόρος: Φωσφόρος, light-bearer, names something that carries light, such as the morning star. The One does not carry light; Athena's word names the light itself.

Whose phrase κάλλος ἀμήχανον does she di.Aristophanes', in the Symposium: Aristophanes tells the myth of the split humans seeking their other half. That is a story of longing between two, not a description of formless beauty at the summit.
Whose phrase κάλλος ἀμήχανον does she di.Timaeus', in the Timaeus: Timaeus speaks of the cosmos and its maker, not of the ladder of love. Athena discusses this phrase with the summit of the ascent in the Symposium.
Whose phrase κάλλος ἀμήχανον does she di.Phaedrus', in the Phaedrus: The Phaedrus does speak of beauty shining through sight, but Athena places this phrase at the top of the ladder of love, where beauty has no shape at all.

Which thinker says the seer was one with.Parmenides: Parmenides says thinking and being are the same, a close cousin of this idea. But the words about the seer and the vision come from a later Platonist.
Which thinker says the seer was one with.Porphyry: Porphyry was Plotinus' pupil and editor, which is why the name tempts. The sentence comes from his teacher's account of union with the One.
Which thinker says the seer was one with.Iamblichus: Iamblichus stressed ritual, theurgy, as the way to the gods. The words about seer and seen being one come from an earlier Platonist's account of union.

Which modern Greek writer called the for.Odysseas Elytis: Elytis is the poet of Aegean light and the Axion Esti. The Abyss as a name for the formless comes from the writer Athena calls the modern Heraclitus.
Which modern Greek writer called the for.Giorgos Seferis: Seferis was a Nobel poet of myth and exile, but the Abyss as the formless is not his term in Athena's talk. It belongs to the author of the Ascetic.
Which modern Greek writer called the for.Konstantinos Cavafy: Cavafy appears in Athena's teaching for Ithaca and the journey home. The bottomless Abyss is the word of a different Greek writer, the author of the Ascetic.

What are the three marks of awakening in.Visions, energy surges and an opened hea: Athena calls awakening an often unnoticed shift of vision, not a show of experiences. Its marks are seen in how one loves and what one stops chasing.
What are the three marks of awakening in.Perfect speech, a fruit diet and a radia: Those are outer signs that can be performed or imitated. Athena's marks are inner: how widely you love, how lightly you live, what you no longer want for yourself.
What are the three marks of awakening in.Silence, solitude and ascetic discipline: Those are practices that may come before awakening, not its marks. Athena even mentions an awakened man with a family and children.

How does awakening arrive, following Soc.κατὰ μικρόν, little by little: Preparation is often long and gradual, but the moment itself is not. Plato's word for it is the one used for the prisoner released without warning.
How does awakening arrive, following Soc.δι' ὀνείρου, through a dream: Dreams belong to the sleep we wake from, so they cannot be the gate. Socrates' word describes the timing of the shift, not its channel.
How does awakening arrive, following Soc.μετὰ θάνατον, after death: Athena insists awakening happens in this life, in the body. Waiting for death confuses physical death with the death of illusion.

According to her, what is the only right.After long ascetic practice: Practice may prepare the ground, but 'first this, then...' is exactly the postponing Athena warns against.
According to her, what is the only right.At the hour of death: That pushes awakening to the end of life. Athena teaches dying to illusion before one dies, not waiting for the last breath.
According to her, what is the only right.At the winter solstice: Athena does say solstices can hasten 'the beautiful hour', which makes this tempting. But they help; they are not the one right moment.

How does she reinterpret the Delphic 'κό.Be polite and well mannered: That is the ordinary sense of κόσμιος, orderly and decent. Athena hears κόσμος in it, the universe, not good manners.
How does she reinterpret the Delphic 'κό.Keep your house in order: Order suits κόσμος, but Athena widens it from the household to the whole. The maxim asks you to recognise what you are, not to tidy what you own.
How does she reinterpret the Delphic 'κό.Obey the laws of the city: Civic obedience reads κόσμιος as merely orderly. Athena takes it beyond the city, to a nature as wide as the cosmos.

Which English word does she say came fro.Idiom: Idiom does come from the same family, ἴδιος, 'one's own', but it names a peculiar way of speaking. The word for the person cut off from the whole is another.
Which English word does she say came fro.Idol: Idol comes from εἴδωλον, an image, a different root entirely. The ἰδιώτης is the private person who cares nothing for the common.
Which English word does she say came fro.Ideal: Ideal comes from ἰδέα, form, Plato's word. The ἰδιώτης is built on ἴδιος, one's own, and English kept it as an insult.

Whom does she contrast with Heraclitus o.Newton: Newton's clockwork universe also left no room for chance, but the line about God and dice belongs to a twentieth-century physicist.
Whom does she contrast with Heraclitus o.Darwin: Darwin gave chance a role in nature, so he is no opponent of the playing child. The 'God does not play dice' line comes from physics.
Whom does she contrast with Heraclitus o.Descartes: Descartes pictured a mechanical world, but he never said God does not play dice. Athena sets Heraclitus against a famous remark about quantum theory.

Where did she film the talk on what awak.The Acropolis of Athens: The Acropolis appears in Athena's teaching as a witness to beauty, but this talk was filmed on a mountain, in winter.
Where did she film the talk on what awak.Delphi: Delphi would suit a talk on awakening, as Apollo's sanctuary, but this one was filmed on a snowy mountain further north.
Where did she film the talk on what awak.Mount Athos: Athos is the monks' mountain of Orthodox Christianity. Athena filmed this talk on the mountain of the old gods.

At which event did she give the talk on.The Galileo Commission conference, 2017: Nothing in Athena's talks links this lecture to the Galileo Commission. It was given in Athens, at a gathering devoted to aromatic arts in ancient Greece.
At which event did she give the talk on.A course on the Orphic Hymns, 2022: Athena does teach the Orphic Hymns, as in the Ares lesson, but this talk was a lecture at a public symposium on aroma, not part of a course.
At which event did she give the talk on.The Palaichthon association in Corinth,: Athena gives other talks for Palaichthon, such as the Corinth lessons on fire and the solstices. This one was in Athens, at a symposium on aroma.

Which Platonic dialogue is her main sour.Theaetetus: The Theaetetus does test the claim that knowledge is perception, so it tempts. But Athena's definition of sensation comes from a dialogue about the cosmos and the soul's circles.
Which Platonic dialogue is her main sour.Phaedo: The Phaedo distrusts the senses as distractions from truth. Athena's account, in which the senses are sacred gates, comes from the dialogue of the soul's circles.
Which Platonic dialogue is her main sour.Philebus: The Philebus weighs pleasure against wisdom. Athena's definition of sensation, waves reaching the soul's circles, comes from Plato's dialogue on the cosmos.

What part of the Cave allegory does she.The fire behind the prisoners: The fire is part of every reading of the Cave, dualist or not. What the dualist reading drops is the ending, after the freed one sees the sun.
What part of the Cave allegory does she.The divided line before it: The Line comes before the Cave, but no reading forgets it. Athena's point is about how the Cave story ends.
What part of the Cave allegory does she.The prisoners' chains at the neck: Everyone remembers the chains; they are the opening image. Athena says the forgotten part comes at the end of the allegory.

Which goddess images the Circle of the S.Athena: Pallas Athena is wisdom born from Zeus's head, not the still centre. The Circle of the Same belongs to the goddess who keeps the hearth.
Which goddess images the Circle of the S.Demeter: Demeter is the mother of grain and of Persephone's return, a goddess of cycles. The Same is what never moves from the centre.
Which goddess images the Circle of the S.Artemis: Artemis roams the wild and, in Athena's reading, is virtue born of Leto. The Circle of the Same is the goddess who stays at the hearth.

With what celestial circles does she com.The Milky Way and the horizon: The Milky Way is a band of stars, and the horizon depends on where you stand. The soul's circles match the two great sky-circles that cross each other.
With what celestial circles does she com.The tropics of Cancer and Capricorn: The tropics are parallel circles, so they never cross. The soul's two circles meet in a χ, as the equator and the ecliptic do.
With what celestial circles does she com.The meridian and the zodiac of Mars: There is no 'zodiac of Mars'. The zodiac lies along the ecliptic, the sun's path, and the Same matches the circle dividing the sky into north and south.

To what does she link the divisions of t.The twelve Olympians: Twelve would suit the signs of the zodiac, but the Timaeus divides the Circle of the Other into seven circles.

To what does she link the divisions of t.The nine Muses: Nine is the Muses' number, not the Other's. The Timaeus divides the Other into seven circles, which Athena pairs with an Eastern teaching.

Who called the soul a 'sentient exhalati.Epicurus: Epicurus made the soul a body of fine atoms spread through the frame. The 'sentient exhalation' is a Stoic definition, from the school's founder.
Who called the soul a 'sentient exhalati.Anaximenes: Anaximenes made air the first principle, so a breath-like soul suits him. But the phrase is Stoic, coined by the founder of the Stoa.
Who called the soul a 'sentient exhalati.Chrysippus: Close: Chrysippus was a later head of the same Stoic school and shared much of this physics. Athena credits the phrase to the school's founder.

What does she say the soul is, 'a verb,.An invisible vessel inside the body: A vessel is a container, a noun, and Athena reverses the picture: the soul is not inside the body; the body is planted in the soul.
What does she say the soul is, 'a verb,.A substance made of fine air: That is closer to the Presocratic or Epicurean soul, a kind of stuff. Athena's soul is not stuff at all but a movement.
What does she say the soul is, 'a verb,.A shadow of the body: That makes the body primary, which Athena reverses: the soul contains the body. And the soul is a motion, not a copy of anything.

Which saying does she quote and extend a.'Man is the measure of all things': That is Protagoras on the relativity of truth, not on how perception works. Athena's saying puts the seeing in the mind, not in the eye.

Which saying does she quote and extend a.'The eye is the lamp of the body': That is from the Gospels, and it puts the light in the eye. Athena's saying moves perception out of the organ and into the mind.

What etymology does she give for φρόνησι.Mind of the midriff (φρένες + νοῦς): That is the plain derivation, from φρένες, the midriff where Homer placed thought. Athena follows the Cratylus instead, which hears motion in the word.
What etymology does she give for φρόνησι.Light of thought (φῶς + νόησις): Light of thought is lovely, and Athena ties σοφία to light. But for φρόνησις Athena follows the Cratylus, where the word is about movement.
What etymology does she give for φρόνησι.Carrying the sacred (φέρω + ὅσιος): Φέρω is close, since the Cratylus reading starts from φορά, motion. But nothing sacred, ὅσιος, is in it; the second part is flow.

What is 'the greatest illness' that righ.ὕβρις and νέμεσις: Hubris and nemesis are tragedy's arrogance and its punishment. The illness right education cures is a state of the mind, not a crime and its payback.
What is 'the greatest illness' that righ.φόβος and λύπη: Fear and grief are passions, the wet and sticky states Athena wants dried out. But the greatest illness is deeper: the soul has forgotten what it is.
What is 'the greatest illness' that righ.ἀκρασία and δειλία: Weakness of will and cowardice are failings of character. The illness paideia cures is a failure of knowing: forgetting and senselessness.

What is the opposite of κόρος (fullness).ἡ πενία, poverty: Poverty is having little, and many poor people are content. Athena notes that many wealthy people are unhappy: the opposite of fullness is a hunger, not a bank balance.
What is the opposite of κόρος (fullness).ἡ ἀπάθεια, impassivity: Ἀπάθεια is Stoic freedom from passion, something Athena values. It is not the opposite of fullness; it is closer to one of its fruits.
What is the opposite of κόρος (fullness).ἡ στέρησις, privation: Στέρησις is lack, having been deprived. Athena's opposite is built on κόρος itself, with a negation: a desire that cannot be filled.

According to Porphyry as she cites him,.The smoke of sacrifices: Porphyry argued against animal sacrifice, and this image is not about offerings. It belongs to his account of heavenly bodies nourished by rising vapours.
According to Porphyry as she cites him,.The light of the stars: The sun gives light rather than taking it from the stars. In Porphyry's image what feeds the heavens rises from below, from water.
According to Porphyry as she cites him,.The breath of living beings: Breath is close to the talk's theme of exhalation, which makes it tempting. But Porphyry's sun feeds on something rising from water, not from creatures.

Which Heraclitean idea closes her talk o.You cannot step into the same river twic: The river fragment is about flux, and Athena does use the river image for the senses. But the talk closes on the soul raised to fire, not on change.

Which Heraclitean idea closes her talk o.Character is destiny: Ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων is about character. The talk on smell ends on a fragment about wetness and dryness, which suits a talk on vapours.

What did her grandmother from Asia Minor.Laurel leaves: Laurel is Apollo's plant, burned at Delphi, but the family custom Athena recalls used the peel of a winter fruit.
What did her grandmother from Asia Minor.Frankincense: Frankincense is the incense of church and temple. Athena's memory is homelier: a fruit peel burned in the house.
What did her grandmother from Asia Minor.Orange blossom: Close, a citrus scent, but blossom is not what was burned. Athena's grandmother burned the peel of a small winter citrus.

What does she say about smell's place in.It is the noblest of the senses: Plato gives that rank to sight, the most sun-like sense. Smell's place in the Timaeus is defined by what it is made of, not by rank.
What does she say about smell's place in.It belongs entirely to fire: Fire in the Timaeus belongs with sight. Smell is a half-formed thing, caught between two other elements.
What does she say about smell's place in.It works without the body: Every sense in the Timaeus works through the body's gates, even if it is the mind that perceives. Smell is defined by its in-between material state.

Whose hymn does she use to close the aro.The Muses: The Muses rule music and memory, but the hymn that leads Persephone up is addressed to the goddesses of the seasons, who bring her back in spring.
Whose hymn does she use to close the aro.The Charites: The Graces are sisters of the Horai, and Athena says they name the same moment as grace. But the hymn that closes the talk is to their sisters, the seasons.
Whose hymn does she use to close the aro.The Nymphs: The Nymphs belong to springs and groves. The hymn Athena closes with is to the goddesses of the seasons and the ripe hour.

What does she call gratitude (εὐγνωμοσύν.The last of the virtues: Athena does end lessons with gratitude, which may suggest 'last'. But Athena calls it what unlocks the other virtues, not what comes after them.
What does she call gratitude (εὐγνωμοσύν.The virtue of slaves: Gratitude is not servility for Athena. It is a heart virtue that activates the good in us and leads the soul toward its purpose.
What does she call gratitude (εὐγνωμοσύν.A mere social courtesy: Courtesy is a habit of manners. For Athena εὐγνωμοσύνη is a heart virtue that aligns the soul with its purpose.

What does φιλότης in φιλοσοφία mean, in.Friendship only: Φιλία can mean friendship, but Athena hears more in φιλότης: a love that wants union, with eros inside it.
What does φιλότης in φιλοσοφία mean, in.Curiosity: Curiosity is a cool interest. Athena's philosophy begins as a love affair, with longing, not mere inquisitiveness.
What does φιλότης in φιλοσοφία mean, in.Respect for teachers: Respect is owed to teachers, but it is not what φιλο- means. The word is about love, and in Athena's reading a burning one.

What was Socrates' practical test of any.τί ἐστι; what is it?: Τί ἐστι, 'what is it?', is Socrates' great question for definitions, and Aristotle's starting point for science. But the test of an inquiry's worth was a different one.
What was Socrates' practical test of any.πόθεν; where from?: Asking where something comes from is a question of origin. Socrates' test was about purpose: what good the inquiry does.
What was Socrates' practical test of any.τίς λέγει; who says so?: 'Who says so?' is an appeal to authority, which Socrates ignored. He cared whether an inquiry served life.

Which example does Aristotle use, as she.A sculptor's marble block: The marble block is the kind of example used for matter shaped from outside by a maker. Entelechy is growth from within.
Which example does Aristotle use, as she.A ship's rudder: A rudder steers from outside. Entelechy is a purpose carried within, in something that grows by itself.
Which example does Aristotle use, as she.A lyre string: A lyre string makes music only when someone plays it. Entelechy is about a living thing unfolding its own end.

What did the Pythagoreans call the fulfi.Release from the body: Release from the body is closer to Plato's Phaedo, and even there Athena reads it as dis-identification. The Pythagorean name is about union, not escape.
What did the Pythagoreans call the fulfi.Return to the Dyad: The Dyad is two, the principle of division. Fulfilment goes the other way, toward the One.
What did the Pythagoreans call the fulfi.Harmony of the spheres: The music of the spheres is a Pythagorean idea about the cosmos, not the name for the fulfilment of a life.

From which verb does she derive μύησις (.μυέω, to teach secrets: Μυέω does mean to initiate, but it is itself built on μύω. Athena goes to the root: shutting eyes and mouth.
From which verb does she derive μύησις (.μῦθος, story: Μῦθος shares the μυ-, and Athena calls mythology an initiation into theology. But μύησις comes from a verb, and story is not its root.

What is her formula from the Republic fo.Knowledge leads to virtue: That is the Socratic thesis that no one does wrong knowingly. Athena's formula is about seeing, with a play on two Greek words one letter apart.

What is her formula from the Republic fo.Order leads to beauty: Order and beauty are Pythagorean themes, but Athena's formula is about vision changing the one who sees.

How does she derive ἐπιστήμη?.ἐπί + στόμα: upon the mouth: Στόμα, mouth, would make knowledge something spoken. Athena's reading is about a standpoint: being above a thing and seeing it whole.
How does she derive ἐπιστήμη?.ἐπί + στῆθος: upon the heart: Στῆθος, chest, would place knowledge in feeling. The root is ἵσταμαι, to stand, which makes ἐπιστήμη a vantage point.
How does she derive ἐπιστήμη?.ἔπος + τιμή: honoured word: Honoured word is a pleasing guess, but it splits the word wrongly. The ἐπι- is a preposition and the rest comes from standing.

Where does the Cave allegory begin?.Republic Book X, 614b: Republic 614b begins the myth of Er, at the very end of the work. The Cave comes earlier, opening Book VII.
Where does the Cave allegory begin?.Timaeus 27c: Timaeus 27c is where Timaeus begins his account of the cosmos, after a prayer to the gods. The Cave is in the Republic.
Where does the Cave allegory begin?.Symposium 210a: Symposium 210a is where Diotima begins the higher mysteries of love, the ladder. That is a different ascent, in a different dialogue.

What are the three allegories of Republi.Cave, Sun, Ring of Gyges: The Ring of Gyges is Glaucon's tale in Book II, far from Books VI and VII. And the Cave comes last of the three, not first.
What are the three allegories of Republi.Myth of Er, Cave, Sun: The Myth of Er closes the Republic in Book X, so it is not one of the three. And the Sun comes first, not last.
What are the three allegories of Republi.Line, Cave, Charioteer: The charioteer belongs to the Phaedrus, not the Republic. In Books VI and VII the Line follows the Sun, and the Cave closes the series.

What does she call the Republic?.'The constitution of the gods': The Republic is a constitution, Πολιτεία, but of the soul and the city, not of the gods. Athena's name for it ranks it as the core sacred text of a whole tradition.
What does she call the Republic?.'The handbook of the Mysteries': Athena does read the Republic as deeply initiatory, which makes this close. But Athena's phrase ranks it as the one scripture of the whole tradition, not a ritual manual.
What does she call the Republic?.'Plato's early sketch': The Republic is a mature work, which Athena calls Plato's magnum opus. Nothing about it is a sketch; it carries the whole tradition.

Who was the last scholarch of the Academ.Proclus: Proclus led the Athenian school about half a century earlier and died in 485. Athena calls him fully awakened, but he did not live to see the closing of 529.
Who was the last scholarch of the Academ.Simplicius: Simplicius was a pupil of Damascius who left Athens with him after the closing. He was a great commentator, not the head of the school.
Who was the last scholarch of the Academ.Olympiodorus: Olympiodorus taught in Alexandria, not Athens, and outlived the closing. The last head of the Athenian school was someone else.

How long did Aristotle study at Plato's.Five years, from 20 to 25: Five years would be a short course. Aristotle stayed far longer, from youth into maturity, until Plato died.
How long did Aristotle study at Plato's.Ten years, from 30 to 40: Aristotle came to Athens as a youth of seventeen, not at thirty, and he left at thirty-seven, when Plato died.
How long did Aristotle study at Plato's.His whole adult life: Aristotle left the Academy after Plato's death and later founded his own school, the Lyceum. His time with Plato had a clear start and end.

What does the sun stand for in the Cave.The body: The body is closer to the cave itself, the tomb the soul lives in. The sun is outside, the source of all light.

How does she put her closing twist on Od.He never reaches Ithaca at all: Odysseus does reach Ithaca; Athena's twist is about how the arrival happens, not whether.

How does she put her closing twist on Od.He chooses Calypso's island instead: Odysseus refuses Calypso's offer of immortality and leaves the island. Athena reads high stations like Calypso's as places to pass through, not to stay.

With what word does she link τροπή (turn.τρόπαιον, trophy: Τρόπαιον, a trophy, does come from τροπή, the turning of the enemy in flight. But Athena's link is about what each turn of the year gives the soul.
With what word does she link τροπή (turn.τρόμος, trembling: Τρόμος, trembling, only sounds similar. Athena's pairing changes a single letter, π to φ, and turns a turning into nourishment.
With what word does she link τροπή (turn.τροχός, wheel: A wheel suits the turning year, which makes it tempting. But Athena's pairing swaps π for φ to find what each turning gives the soul.

In her reading, whom does infant Zeus, n.The physical sun: Athena does not read infant Zeus as the sun. Zeus in Athena's teaching is consciousness, the cosmic mind, and the myth speaks of our own.
In her reading, whom does infant Zeus, n.The body's appetites: Appetites belong to the Titans' pull in Athena's reading, not to Zeus. Zeus is the highest power in us, hidden and nursed until it can rule.
In her reading, whom does infant Zeus, n.The city's lawgiver: The lawgiver is a political figure. Athena reads the infant god inwardly: a power of awareness in us, nursed in secret.

From which words does she derive δαίμων?.δαίς (feast) and μένος (force): Δαίς, a feast, does share the δαι- sound, but Athena hears knowing and burning in δαίμων, not banqueting and strength.
From which words does she derive δαίμων?.δεῖμα (fear) and ὤν (being): Δεῖμα, fear, would make the daimon a frightening being, close to the Christian demon Athena rejects. For Athena the daimon is the inner true self.
From which words does she derive δαίμων?.δέω (bind) and μοῖρα (fate): Binding and fate suggest a daimon that chains you to your lot. Athena's daimon frees: it is the inner teacher, the self that knows.

Why does she say εὐτυχία is not εὐδαιμον.It belongs only to the gods: Athena says εὐτυχία is real for humans, just unreliable. The trouble is not who can have it but that it can be lost.
Why does she say εὐτυχία is not εὐδαιμον.It is a purely bodily pleasure: Good fortune covers far more than the body: money, success, relationships. Its weakness is that circumstances give it and circumstances take it away.
Why does she say εὐτυχία is not εὐδαιμον.It can only be found after death: Good fortune comes in this life, and often. Athena's point is that it turns: today's luck can be tomorrow's misfortune.

What does Proclus' ideal of the 'naked s.A soul without a body after death: Athena insists the stripping happens in this life, while in the body. Nakedness means taking off identifications, not the flesh.
What does Proclus' ideal of the 'naked s.A soul that has given up the senses: Athena teaches that the senses are purified and kept as allies, not given up. What is removed are the roles we wrongly take for ourselves.
What does Proclus' ideal of the 'naked s.A soul with no memories: Losing memories is not the point; the soul's memory, μνημοσύνη, is something Athena wants awakened. What falls away are the false 'I am this' layers.

Why are we colder in winter though Earth.Because the sun's fire weakens: The sun burns as strongly all year. Athena's reading needs this: from the sun's own point of view there is no waxing or waning.
Why are we colder in winter though Earth.Because the moon blocks the light: The moon blocks the sun only in an eclipse, and briefly. The seasons come from the Earth's tilt, which Athena reads as the soul's stance.
Why are we colder in winter though Earth.Because winter clouds absorb the heat: Clouds vary from place to place and cannot explain a season across a whole hemisphere. The cause is the angle at which sunlight falls.

What does she say philosophers called νῦ.A name of Kronos: Kronos is linked with χρόνος, time, the flow of before and after. The now stands outside that flow, and the philosophers gave it the name of the god of light.

What does she say philosophers called νῦ.The shadow of eternity: That would make the now a pale copy, the way time is an image of eternity. Athena treats the now as full light, not a shadow.

From which verb does she derive the Tita.τίνω, to pay a penalty: Τίνω, to pay a penalty, sounds close, and Hesiod even hints at vengeance to come. But Athena takes the Neoplatonic link to stretching: the Titans as our tensions.

From which verb does she derive the Tita.τιμάω, to honour: Τιμάω, to honour, has nothing to do with the Titans' role in Athena's reading. They are the forces that pull us out into becoming.

According to Porphyry as she cites him,.Enter through Leo, exit through Aquarius: Leo and Aquarius are not solstice signs. Porphyry's two gates sit at the year's turning points, the solstices.
According to Porphyry as she cites him,.Enter through Virgo, exit through Pisces: Virgo and Pisces lie at neither solstice. The gates of souls in Porphyry are the two signs where the sun turns back.

How does Plato define time, as she quote.The measure of motion: Measuring motion is how clocks and later physics treat time. Plato's line in the Timaeus defines time by what it images: something that does not move.
How does Plato define time, as she quote.The number of change: That echoes Aristotle, who defines time as the number of motion. Plato's definition, the one Athena quotes, relates time to eternity, not to counting.
How does Plato define time, as she quote.The river of becoming: A river suits Heraclitus and becoming, but it is not Plato's definition. Plato defines time by its relation to eternity, as its image.

What happens in the soul at a 'psychic e.The soul leaves the body: Nothing leaves the body at an equinox. Athena's psychic equinox is a meeting inside the soul.
What happens in the soul at a 'psychic e.The two circles are farthest apart: That is the psychic solstice, the greatest distance between our true nature and life in becoming. The equinox is the opposite.
What happens in the soul at a 'psychic e.The Circle of the Same stops turning: The Circle of the Same never stops; it is the steady centre. At the equinox the two circles come together.
